 Midnight purple, playing cards and farmer kings: The Diwali box gets a second life
 The red and gold were never the problem. The fifth identical box in the pile was. Six brands, from a donut maker in midnight purple to a skincare label with a Ludo board, on why the best Diwali packaging is the kind you cannot bring yourself to bin. 
 By   Sakshi Dhingra | November 7, 2026, 10:41:02 IST Share Share this Article
 × WhatsApp Facebook Twitter Linkedin Mail 
 Follow Us 
 How brands are giving festive gift boxes a second life Walk into any Diwali gifting season and you will meet the same box: red, gold, a diya in one corner, rangoli in another. It is a perfectly respectable box. It is also, as Tarak Bhattacharya, CEO and Executive Director of Mad Over Donuts, puts it, forgettable by the time you reach the fifth. "Nobody remembers the fifth identical box in the pile." No design brief has said it more efficiently.
 His own fix is deep midnight purple, scattered with gold foil stars and fireworks. He insists on keeping what matters. "Diwali has a dress code," he says, so the gold and the glow stay. What goes is the sameness. He is also happy to say what other brands tiptoe around. A festive box is photographed before it is tasted, and "any brand that says otherwise isn’t being candid." Then comes the line worth underlining: "the camera only wins the first look." What brings people back is the donut inside, and the Diwali Luxe Edit is built for that. Bhattacharya says it is "made to be devoured", with three handcrafted, 100% vegetarian donuts: Hazelnut Sparkle, Ivory Cashew Indulgence and Signature Almond Crumble.
 Deconstruct wanted its box to do something, and landed on Ludo. Somya Bhargava, Senior Vice President and Head of Brand and Marketing, calls it "a game that cuts across generations", which makes it a fair stand-in for the festival itself. The packaging comes with dice and tokens, and the hamper holds four bestsellers: a Gel Sunscreen, a 5% Vitamin C Gel Sunscreen, a Brightening Lip Balm and an Oil-Free Moisturiser. This may be the first time a sunscreen has been asked to referee a family game night.
 Two Brothers India Farms went to the field. Ashwin Shetty, VP Growth and Digital Marketing, describes a festive range called MAAN, in blue, green and brown instead of red and gold, with illustrations of the people who grow, harvest and process the food. The three hampers are named for them. Annadata is for the farmers, Anaajkaar for the people who turn the harvest into ingredients, and Annapurna for the women who prepare the festive treats. The Annapurna box holds Khapli Mathri, Shankarpali, Kaju Katli, Khajoor Laddoo and banana chips, along with cultured ghee, Kashmiri saffron and spiced jaggery for the home kitchen. Every hamper also carries The Harvest Deck, a pack of Diwali-themed playing cards where the farmer is the king. At last, the person who grows the food outranks everyone at the table.

 Canva Layoffs Kuku Technologies MIB OTT Advisory Jill Hazelbaker Helen Chiang Shetty remembers Diwali as the time families made faral at home and shared it with neighbours, and wants the hamper to bring that feeling back. On the camera, his position is clear: "a hamper should offer something beyond a good photograph." Demand, he says, has grown compared with last year. 
 SEVA Home turned to artists. Arushi Agrawal, Founder and Director, sums up the approach in one line: "We kept the warmth and the sense of ritual, and left out the literal." With Suryakant Lokhande, the brand made The Playing Cards Edit and The Mahjong Edit, each a set of four individually illustrated scented candles. In the cards edition the King, Queen, Jack and Ace become collectibles, paired with NOIR, a fragrance inspired by Diwali after dark. With Payal Singhal came candle and diffuser gift sets and closet fresheners. The Jasmine set has been a clear favourite, and the Chintz print has had customers sending photos of it styled on their consoles and dining tables. Some have come back for a second set for themselves after gifting the first.
 The review Agrawal treasures most is the one about recipients who "didn’t want to light them straight away because they looked too beautiful", and then did. It is rare for a product to be praised for being too good-looking to use, and then praised again for being used.
 Saffron & Mishri, founded by Gunjan Shrivastava, treats the box as a canvas. Shrivastava trained in visual arts, and sees food through colour, composition, texture and story. She is careful not to dismiss tradition, noting that Indian festivities have a visual language of their own. Her point is that "tradition doesn't have to look the same every year." The aim is packaging that feels like "something people would want to hold on to even after the sweets are gone."
 SMOOR, whose CMO is Kanchan Anchpal, begins from a simple rule: "No two Diwalis look the same at SMOOR." This year's theme is a "United Diwali", a way of saying thank you and celebrating togetherness. The curation pairs signature chocolates and gourmet treats with handwoven baskets, brass diyas and reusable trays. The hamper it is proudest of is the Handwoven Festive Sustainable Hamper, made with Industree Foundation, which works with rural women and women-owned producer enterprises. The idea is that the joy of the season reaches the communities behind the gift.
 Look across the six and the pattern is hard to miss. Nobody threw tradition out. Gold survives, diyas survive, and the festival is still the point. What changed is the idea of the box as a wrapper to be torn open, photographed and recycled within the hour. A deck of cards, a board game, a candle, a basket, a tray and a canvas all say the same thing: the box should stay.
 The smartest Diwali packaging this season is the kind you cannot throw away without feeling faintly rude.
